utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Would you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning to you. This is case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm still John Ackerman with my colleagues, Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good morning to you. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. First of all, can I deal with the witness. Yesterday, I realised when I was going through the documents that it is almost impossible for this man to give evidence in open session even with a pseudonym and voice distortion and for him not to be identified because everything he says identifies him, as to who he is. I spoke to him this morning and as I understand it, he is prepared now to testify in open session. The only alternative would have been complete closed session, I think, because we would have been in and out the whole time of closed or private session. The only thing -- because I only appreciated this yesterday afternoon, I spoke to him briefly this morning but I think it may be as well if we start in private session while Your Honour just confirms with him that he is content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I was going to suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that must be the right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not that I don't take your word. Don't misunderstand me. It's just to make sure he knows exactly what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly Your Honour, and regrettably when I arranged to see him this morning at 8.30 I forgot to organise an interpreter so we had to wait so it was a bit rushed. Your Honour, but can I deal with some other matters first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first is this: Your Honours, in respect of the progress or shortening of the case, we have taken a decision that we will not be leading evidence now in respect of three municipalities. That is to say, Bosanska Dubica, Bosanska Gradiska, and Bihac/Ripac. In addition, we will almost certainly be reducing the evidence on some of the smaller municipalities, although we will be calling some evidence. We told Your Honours sometime ago that in relation to some municipalities, we would be reducing the witness to one and I think in others as well but that's still not finalised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And regarding Prijedor? Yesterday I inquired, you were not here at the time, but I inquired to Mr. Ackerman who said he was preparing a draft joint memo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes he was. It was given to me yesterday after court. Your Honours, I have not had a chance to consider it carefully. I think probably it will be an agreed document. It's just a question of I just want to make sure that I understand exactly what is being suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Okay. When that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say this? Subject to things not going wrong and us being out on our timing, we estimate we will be starting Prijedor next Monday, Monday week, it may well be that we will in fact have a free day on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Monday, 21st, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, we will be starting Prijedor on Monday the 21st. We will finish with Kljuc next week. There is a problem that has arisen over the Rule 92 witnesses, which I want to bring to Your Honour's attention now. The -- our estimate is that we will finish Prijedor by Christmas, on the basis that there will be very few witnesses who will be giving evidence in full. In other words, going through the whole saga. One of the problems with that is of course this: There are a large number of relevant documents that relate to Prijedor. I think Your Honours have been given the binders. Yes. In advance. And many of the witnesses dealt with those documents in their previous evidence. I think I will at some stage be asking Your Honours to perhaps take a day just to read through the documents that are in there because we won't be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman will love that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, not in court. I've given that one up. But there really are a huge number of relevant -- when if Your Honours are going to read the transcripts in advance you're going to need to look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We take them -- we do read them as we go along obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. All right. Your Honour, I think that deals with the question of as it were timing. The best guess that we can give at the moment is that the Prosecution case will finish before the Easter break. That is certainly the target we are aiming for. Your Honour, in respect of Prijedor, there is one other matter. In the Stakic case, Judge Schomburg - I'm sorry - the Trial Chamber, the Judges of their own volition, called a witness from Prijedor, a man named Baltic. He was the secretary to the Prijedor Crisis Staff. He's not on the witness list because in a sense, he's not -- he wasn't a Prosecution witness at all. And therefore he didn't come under as it were Prosecution witnesses. But it may well be that we will be calling him in this trial again. We are going to hand over the transcripts of what he said. The only reason I put it at this stage with a query is nobody has actually spoken to him as to his willingness to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stakic, he is not a witness of the Prosecution, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No he was called by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You intend to make him become one in this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In one sense, Your Honour, yes, in the sense that he would be put in to give evidence again with -- as it were, as part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But as I say, one of the difficulties is he wasn't a Prosecution witness and he's never been contacted by the Prosecution. So that's why we have to make certain inquiries. Your Honour, can I come now then to the Rule 92 aspect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask the usher, please, to go to the witness and explain to him that we are dealing with procedural matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I told him that in advance Your Honour. I said he wouldn't be likely to get on before 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because I knew I had these matters to raise. Your Honours gave a ruling on the Rule 92 on the 3rd of September of this year. And one of the witnesses -- can I just find it? Witness 7.192, was not opposed on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin but was the Defence for Talic at that stage required his attendance. And Your Honours then ruled that he should attend and cross-examination by counsel for Talic would be limited to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Your Honour, this witness was seen yesterday in the area in which he lives, because he in fact is ill, not ill but has a heart condition, which makes it impossible for him to travel to The Hague. Your Honour, the medical certificate is being faxed through this morning and I can produce it tomorrow. But in respect of that witness, as it was that Mr. Brdjanin didn't wish to cross-examine him in any event, we are going to be asking that in the light of his health, the statement should go in without cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were a lot of matters raised and I guess I'll start with the last one since it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As I told Your Honours on more than one occasion, up until the severance, there was a lot of joint Defence going on between us and the Talic Defence and for instance with regard to this 92 bis issue, I knew that the Talic Defence was going to request the witness be brought here for cross-examination and it would have been surplusage and a waste of time for me to make the same motion and that's why I didn't. That doesn't mean that I didn't want him brought here for cross-examination at the initial instance just because I didn't ask for it doesn't mean that I wasn't interested in it. And it didn't make much difference to me whether it was the Talic Defence team that cross-examined him or me. I don't know if his condition is any different now than it was in September when the matter was first brought here but I doubt it. I presume that he was in the same condition then. It was not -- I don't know whether it was raised at that time or how it was dealt with. But I want to take advantage in every case where it was -- we had a joint situation with the Talic Defence team, where they made objections or requests that I agreed with, that I not lose the benefit of those just because there has been a severance. Therefore, I maintain the position that I said in my communication to Ms. Korner of a few days ago, that this person should be brought here for cross-examination. And part of that, Your Honour, is based on the proposition that I have requested earlier in this case for some guidance and clarification regarding the application of 92 bis which the Court was -- the Chamber was reluctant to extend. And therefore, I still do not have any guidance as to how the Chamber will treat Rule 92 bis statements. And so I must assume they will be treated in the way -- in a way that is not particularly helpful to my client. With regard to the Stakic case, or the Prijedor part of this case, I learned late yesterday that it was the intention of the Prosecution to try to start the Prijedor phase of this case a week from Monday. We were handed the witness list and the exhibit list yesterday morning. There are, I don't know, 500 exhibits maybe on the list. We haven't even had a chance to count them. I was also told that the first witness they want to bring is probably the most complicated in terms of the amount of transcript material that has to be dealt with, with regard to that witness. I cannot imagine how we can in any way be prepared to deal with that much material, that complicated a situation, become familiar with all of these exhibits, to make our objections regarding these exhibits, to be prepared to start the Prijedor phase of this case until what we were originally told it would be, and that would be around the end of the month. So my humble request Your Honour is that we not start the Prijedor phase of this case until the 28th of this month, Monday, the 28th, because I can't possibly be ready before that then. I just don't know how I can. You have not probably seen the universe of material that I have to deal with Your Honour but it's just staggering. And I can't do that over a weekend. I can't do it in a day or two. It takes several days to get even close to being ready for that. So that's my request. The -- one of the effects of the severance is we have clearly speeded this case up a rather dramatic amount. The Prosecutor just told you that she thinks we could finish as early as the Easter break next year which is I think substantially ahead of where we thought we were going to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In any event, I really would be terribly handicapped if we had to go forward with the Prijedor case a week from Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think I'll deal with that first Your Honour and then go back to Rule 92 because I hadn't finished before Mr. Ackerman got up. There is another problem. Your Honour, there are a number of issues relating to this. I understand of course that the complication of Prijedor is the amount of previous material for some of the witnesses. But the fact is those witnesses will be called very shortly, so it's not a question of there having to be a lengthy examination-in-chief now. If we don't start until the 28th, then it will not finish before Christmas. Today, after -- at some stage during the day, Mr. Ackerman is going to be given the documents relating to a witness who has had a witness summons served on him, who relates to Kljuc, and that's going to interrupt the Prijedor flow in any event. I raise it now because of Mr. Ackerman's request. If we start on the 28th only, we are going to lose the week of November the 4th, very largely I would think, to this witness. In addition to that, we have a further usual complication that at the moment the Defence case is going to start in Stakic on the 18th of November. I understand a new Judge has been found. I have -- we will be making a request to delay that start in any event but we are going to have the very unhappy situation of Prosecution witnesses and Defence witnesses in the Prijedor case being in this building together, apart from anything else they may be staying in the same places. So I'm very anxious to get Prijedor started on the 21st. Mr. Ackerman, I understand the problems, but Mr. Ackerman does have a co-counsel. I've heard what he says he doesn't want the co-counsel to take over but there is a co-counsel here to assist in the preparation for witnesses, and a legal assistant. Therefore, I would suggest that there is sufficient time between now and then to prepare for the witnesses that will come that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we use the week profitably doing something else?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. There isn't anything else we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no -- Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Trbojevic is a highly capable lawyer but he cannot read those transcripts and there are no transcripts in B/C/S, and therefore, his assistance in that regard getting that material together is just not possible. Please understand that just because we are not sitting in this Court doesn't mean that we are not making progress and if we didn't start Prijedor until the 28th, then that among other things would probably keep me from standing up and saying to you, "I can't be prepared for tomorrow, let's take a day off tomorrow." One of the things that is going to happen because of what I think is going to be our agreement regarding Prijedor is where there might have been four days of direct examination, there might be a half of a day or a day, which means that the witnesses will move -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Mr. Ackerman. I'm thinking of a possible solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With the way that we are probably going to handle Prijedor by using the transcripts, it means the witnesses will move through the process much more rapidly than they otherwise would have, which has among other things, the effect of reducing the amount of time that would be available to me for preparation of their cross-examination. And that's an additional problem and the preparation time is going to have to be found, whether we do it during the week of the 21st or do it sporadically as we go along working like three days a week instead of five, that it's just going to have to happen that way. I can't imagine, Your Honour, that there is any excuse for the Prosecutor having waited until yesterday to give us the exhibit lists and the witness list. I just can't imagine there is any excuse for that, and I can only think it was deliberately done to make it more difficult for us to be prepared because they had to have known for weeks the exhibits they were going to use in Prijedor and the witnesses they were going to use in Prijedor and it was only when I sent an e-mail saying, you have not given us this, we can't possibly get prepared without it, that I got it the next day, and if it's the Prosecutor's wish that we move efficiently in this case, then she ought not to wait until the very last minute to give us materials like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I really don't know why it's necessary each time for Mr. Ackerman to insinuate that the Prosecution is behaving dishonourably, deliberately. The reason for the delay was twofold: First, we went back through the exhibits after General Talic disappeared from this case, to see if we could reduce the number. That was one of the reasons Your Honour gave us a week off. As regards the witnesses, the Stakic case only finished something over a week ago and we had to assess at the end of the day which witnesses we were going to call and that is the reason. I am a touch troubled that Mr. Ackerman in the light of the way we've conducted the case so far, thinks that we are deliberately trying to make life more difficult for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I just off the cuff make a suggestion? I know that I ought actually to first discuss it with my colleagues but before I do so, perhaps I could get a feedback from you. The week of the 21st to the 25th of October, already contains two days in which we are not working. That's Thursday, the 24th of October, which is an United Nations holiday, and Friday, the 25th of October, which is a court maintenance. Yes, yes. Definitely. So we are talking of three days during that week. 21st and 22nd we are working in the morning, we are sitting in the morning, 23rd we are sitting in the afternoon. 24th, 25th, we are not sitting. In November, we had scheduled a break of which you are all aware, basically starting from the 19th -- from the 13th, restarting then on the 25th. May I suggest, and then we discuss it obviously because I am saying this off the cuff, and I don't know what the position of the other two Judges is, that we eliminate the last three days of that break, that is the 20th, 21st and 22nd, and work those three days? We would resume instead of on the 25th, in other words we would resume on the 20th, 23rd and 24th are Saturday and Sunday but again this is subject of course to Judge Taya and Judge Janu being able to do that. I mean, I will be going to Malta and will be returning on the 19th so I can actually resume on the 20th, straight away. So in other words, we eliminate three days in October and we gain three days in November. If that is -- I think that should try to -- I'm trying to meet you halfway and sort of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I tell you what effect that will have. And that is that the order of witnesses will have to be reorganised again because we are trying to have the same persons calling the witnesses as called them in Stakic. And the first witness was the one I dealt with. I will not be here at all the week of the 28th. I have professional commitments in London.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 28th of October?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of October. So in that event I think it's a matter for Your Honours to decide upon. It would be preferable in my view not to be crossing over Stakic with this case again but I've made the point. But then, if Your Honours go for that, then the order of witnesses will not be the same. So we will have to have another look at it. I'm just saying that so Mr. Ackerman doesn't think we are deliberately trying to throw the Defence out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Beside, apart from that, because I wouldn't even try to get --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just saying Your Honour that's the consequence that will have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I suggest to you that you take advantage of the first break that we will have to further discuss it amongst yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't actually think that -- my application is that we stick to the old schedule. Mr. Ackerman is that we don't. And I think it's as simple as that and it's a matter for Your Honours to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Having put us in that position, we will have to decide. We would have preferred if you could have sat down and come to an agreement between you, amongst you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I mean, Mr. Ackerman doesn't want to sit the 21st, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but exactly. When I say I suggest you sit down, each party has to depart from a position of rigidity and assume that there can be some flexibility and some sort of adjustment. Perhaps I understand what your problem is. Mr. Ackerman is keeping silent. But this is why I'm saying that perhaps you could take five minutes during the first break and see if you can come to some sort of agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we can but at the moment we are poles apart and the only agreement -- I don't see Mr. Ackerman saying I'll sit on the 21st. And we are saying, fine, we prefer to sit on the 21st but Your Honours can rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also heard Mr. Ackerman complain that -- not complain but mention that the fact as to who is going to be the first witness worries him a little bit by way of having to prepare, finalise his preparations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or be prepared so perhaps if you could -- this is why I'm saying do meet, take five minutes, because the moment you leave -- you ought to negotiate, doors start opening and then you see whether it's feasible or not. But if you don't want to, I mean we will take a decision. But then it will be a decision which probably none of you will like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, somebody is going to like it Your Honour. But -- may I say all the early witnesses would virtually be the same. They have all got because they are the witnesses that cover the political background in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could in fact be back to resume sitting on the 21st but I'll only say this about that. It's not totally helpful to give me three days preparation time and then take three days preparation time away from me later which I had planned to use for the very purpose of doing Prijedor matter. But it may -- it might make sense to do what you suggest and just see where we are when we get to that point. We can certainly, by using the three days that you've offered next week, get to the point by the 28th where we will be ready to go with at least the initial phases of the Prijedor case. And if that goes along smoothly and we can come back on the 21st without any problem and keep going, then so be it, we've solved the problem and we may -- that may very well work and it may not, but I'm certainly willing to try that and I think it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't think Your Honour was offering three days next week. Your Honour said the three days of the 21st should be off, not next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, not next week, no. Next week we are working the whole week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. That's how I understood you anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As it transpires, I think in any event that there will be spare time next week. I don't think we will certainly be using the Friday and probably not Thursday because what I was going to say, was that Witness 7.117, who was a witness -- a Rule 92 witness that Your Honour said should attend for cross-examination by both counsel won't attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have one witness less?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So Your Honour next week, subject to the next witness finishing on Monday, on Tuesday, we have -- and maybe starting on Monday, I can't remember the numbers but he's a witness who Mr. Ackerman has already prepared for in fact because he was supposed to come sometime ago when General Talic felt ill. Then we have one witness from Sanski Most and two of the witnesses -- the Rule 92 witnesses that were asked for. So it should only be half an hour each on Your Honour's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Ms. Korner to get either Ms. Gustin or someone prepare us a tentative time schedule for the witnesses that will -- the evidence that we will be hearing next week?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that I can perhaps do something, work on that, and either -- just prepare that and then we'll discuss it because I think it can give us an opportunity to offer something else as well. So -- all right. If you could let us have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By the end of today sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much you anticipate, in other words, because then I can turn it on Mr. Ackerman and more or less I can also get an indication of how much they intend to dedicate to each of these witnesses, and perhaps we can have a day or two off next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, as far as I can see, Friday will certainly be off, and possibly part of Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- okay. I just appeal to you to be it as practical as possible and please do approach each other in a positive way rather than making allegations or assertions of this and of that. I mean, it's -- we are ourselves taking the approach that we consider both of you to be cooperative and if possible, we would like to avoid having to fix time limits for the Prosecution or time limits for the Defence. We prefer to adopt a system whereby you yourself realise what's necessary for your case and you will have ample space or the space necessary to conduct your case as you feel you should be conducting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour I did raise that I think sometime ago because as I said, and I've said more than once in this case, if there's any question that an arbitrary time limit will be set, then I need to know that well in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the idea, Ms. Korner, I mean we are being very plain and very straightforward with you because this is something that we have been discussing. We do not believe that you have bee abusing the process. It's true that some examination -- direct examination could have been shorter. It's true that some questions could have been avoided. But in reality, I think you've been extremely considerate in what you have brought forward. And I have no reason to doubt that the same approach will be forthcoming from the Defence. So the attitude we try to adopt is not to foreclose on you. Because otherwise, it's a system which I personally don't like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but nobody can fail to be unaware of the public sentiments that have been expressed by President Jorda as to the length of time trials are lasting and therefore that's why my anxiety is to make sure that if I am to be given an arbitrary deadline I know well in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is a difficult case. It's one of the perhaps most voluminous cases and one of the most difficult cases that one can imagine. It was anticipated in the very beginning it would last at least a year and a half in any case, so I don't think any one can say that we are unduly protracting this case or -- I think we have gone ahead pretty much efficiently and when I have been asked, this is what I have stated. But I have no reason to complain as to the way, until now at least, the Prosecution has conducted its case and I have no reason to believe that the Defence will provide or opt for obstacles or a negative -- so shall we bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually better be closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How easy it is to go into closed session in this courtroom because.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the same?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we better go into closed session for a while. I'll explain to the witness what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please go next to the witness. May I ask you to stand up, please? So good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are here to give evidence in this case against Radoslav Brdjanin and according to the rules before you proceed with your testimony, you are required to enter, to make a solemn declaration before this Tribunal that in the course of your testimony, you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. It's the equivalent of an oath. The text of the solemn declaration is contained in a document which will be handed to you now by the usher, and my request to you is to kindly read it out aloud. That will be your solemn undertaking to us that you will be speaking the truth and the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. I know that you were informed earlier on this morning that although you were being brought here before 9.00 we would not be summoning you into the courtroom immediately, but that there will be a delay. I apologise to you on behalf of the Tribunal. The reason is that we had several procedural matters to attend to before your testimony could commence, procedural matters that have absolutely nothing to do with you, they have to do with the proper running of the case, but as a result of them, we couldn't bring you in to start with your evidence at 9.00 as we would have liked to. Next thing I wanted to tell you is who we are. I am the Presiding Judge and I am flanked by Judge Janu to my right and Judge Taya to my left. Judge Janu comes from the Czech Republic, Judge Taya from Japan and I come from the tiny island of Malta. To your right is the team for the Prosecution headed by Ms. Joanna Korner with whom you are familiar. You're right is over there, sir. Don't do like me. And to your left, the front row, there is the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin headed by lead counsel, John Ackerman. Procedure that will be followed is a very simple one. You will be first asked a series of questions by the Prosecution. And when that is over, then the accused, through his counsel, has got a right to cross-examine you. That is to put questions to you. Your position with regard to the parties, that is Prosecution and Defence, as far as questions are concerned, must be a neutral one. You have just promised us to tell us the truth it and therefore, you have a duty to answer all questions that are put it to you, irrespective of whether they are coming from the Prosecution or the Defence. You have to right to distinguish between the Prosecution and the Defence saying that the Prosecution are my friend, the Defence are not my friends or anything like that. You have a duty to answer all questions, unless we tell you not to answer a particular question. I also want to put your mind at rest that we are always on the lookout to make sure that the questions that are put to you are questions that are allowed by the law which is contained in our -- in other words, there will be no questions allowed which the rules protect you against. All right? With that, I give the floor to Ms. Korner who can proceed with the first question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm advised to say that Ms. Korner comes from a medium-sized island.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, is your name Asim Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you born on the 27th of July of 1952?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you, by nationality, and ethnicity, a Bosniak, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, Mr. Egrlic, a number of questions as you know about the events of 1991 and 1992, in Kljuc, but first of all I just want to go through the various statements or documents that you've signed during the course of these events. I think it's right that you made your first statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1997.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you make a further statement in March of 2001?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In addition to that, before you were seen by the Office of the Prosecutor, were you interviewed and made statements to the authorities in the -- in Bosnia, in 1994, 1995, and 1996?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, on the question of documents, were you interviewed after your detention by the Serb authorities in Kljuc in the police station and later when you were sent to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come to the circumstances of your interviews -- those interviews when we deal with it. Now, can I go back, please, to 1990? Did you join the, as it were, new party, the SDA, before the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I joined just before the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in the 1990 elections in Kljuc, is this right, that the Serb party, the Serb nationalist party, the SDS, won more seats than the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was your position in the SDA in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I was president of the executive board of the SDA for Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was the leader of the SDA in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I was the leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. I'm sorry so you as the president of the executive board were also the leader?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was there also another Muslim party in the Kljuc municipality namely the MBO?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: There was, the Muslim Bosniak Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And was that headed by Omer Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After the elections, when I think the SDA were the -- was the second party, did the SDS assume the positions of first of all president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was the gentleman who was president, Jovo Banjac?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you become the president of the executive board of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Omer Filipovic become the vice-president of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, up until the war started in Croatia in 1991, what were relationships like between the ethnicities in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: They were satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What difference did the outbreak of war in Croatia make?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The security situation changed in the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Volunteers from the Croatian war front were returning and disturbing the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you say "disturbing," what were they actually doing?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: They were armed, and out of control, with a lot of ammunition. They would open fire on settlements and they started looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When mobilisation was ordered for the war in Croatia, did the Muslims in Kljuc respond to that mobilisation order?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: They did not respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what effect did that failure to respond have on relations between the ethnicities in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: This divided and upset relationships that used to exist among the political parties in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's now look at the political parties. Up until that time, in 1991, what was the relationship between the SDS and the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: They were quite good. We cooperated in the work of the assembly, and we did our normal duties, in a normal atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you personally acquainted with, first of all, Mr. Banjac?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I knew him personally, because before, we used to work together for about ten years in a construction company called Sana-Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some other people in the SDS. Veljko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What position did he hold during this period, that is 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: He was first the secretary of the municipal assembly and after that, he was chief of the police station in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what about Vinko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Veljko Kondic, was president of the SDS in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I thought. I think there is -- it's probably my pronunciation, Mr. Egrlic. The first person I asked you was in fact Veljko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. And he was the President of the SDS for Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And had you worked with him before the creation of the political parties?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have a good relationship with Mr. Veljko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We had a good relationship and we cooperated well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now, finally, it's Vinko Kondic, was he the one who was chief of the police station?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And had you known him before --

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I had, I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of those three men, who held the, if you like, the most nationalist views?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I think Vinko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did he express those views?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It was very hard to come to any agreement with him on many issues that were of common interest, because he advocated only the positions of the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask now about the SDS and -- in Kljuc and any links it may have had with other areas. Did you hear of Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I had heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When did you first become aware of Radoslav Brdjanin as a person?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: He was a well-known figure in the media because he frequently appeared on television as a deputy in the assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of any other political position that he held? And I'm dealing now entirely with 1991, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Later on, he held the position of president of the autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When did you first hear of the autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I heard of it for the first time in the second half of 1991, when the proposal was presented at the municipal assembly that we should take a vote in favour of Kljuc municipality joining that region.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who proposed that Kljuc should join the region?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The president of the assembly, Jovo Banjac, proposed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the view of your party towards joining the autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Our party did not accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Because that meant establishing an autonomy and bodies of authority within Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was an internationally recognised state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the result of that proposal to join the autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The result was that the municipal assembly stopped functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Because we, from the SDA, did not agree with such a decision, and under those conditions, we could not continue working in the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Over what period of time did the discussions about joining the autonomous region go on?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The discussions went on from the second half of 1991, and the final decision was taken in April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you were aware of Mr. Brdjanin on television because he was prominent because of his position as a deputy in the assembly, and later, as president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. At what stage did you become aware that, as you say, he was president of the autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I learnt that in the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you become aware of any connection between Mr. Brdjanin and the SDS in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you become aware of that connection?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: There was cooperation between the Kljuc SDS and higher bodies within the SDS organisation at the level of the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you find out about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I found out on the basis of certain decisions taken by the SDS and which were in accordance with the decisions of higher levels of authority of the SDS in the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was there anything in particular that made you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a telex which I happened to receive among the mail that I received regularly as president of the executive board of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you received that telex, did you keep it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I showed it to Mr. Jovo Banjac as the president of the assembly and as my work colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to have a look, please, at a document marked P22. Now, this is a telex dated the 29th of October, 1991, and it says, "Please deliver this telex to the president of the municipal assembly. Thank you. Order of the SDS in Sarajevo, which was made public at the meeting of all the municipal presidents on the 26th of November, 1991, at 1500 hours in Banja Luka, chaired by Dr. Karadzic and which was fully accepted at the session of the Presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner said 26 November, 1991. The document I have says 26 October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right I was going to correct you on that, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine. I think we can see it on the screen, if I mispronounced it, so be it, but the document is there. And then there is a list of instructions, one through to 14, and finally it says at the bottom, "Celinac, 29th of October, 1991," and signed, or the subscription is coordinator for implementing decisions, Radoslav Brdjanin, vice-president of the assembly of the autonomous region. Now, is this the telex that you received whilst you were in the municipal building and about which you spoke to Mr. Banjac?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you in fact yourself keep a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what happened to the copy that you kept?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, my house was set on fire and all the documents I had burnt, including that copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said that you spoke to Mr. Banjac about this. What did you say to him or what was the conversation about this document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I asked him what it was about, what kind of a document this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was his reply?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: He said, "Never mind that. Brdjo is crazy."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he say anything more about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: He didn't say anything more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are in there a set of instructions. Were those instructions actually put into effect?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All of them or just some of them, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Most of them were implemented, from 1991 right up until May, 1992, that is as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. You can put that document away. Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. Now, you said that Mr. Banjac talked about this document by saying that Brdjo was mad. Did you have any other conversations with any of the leadership of the SDS about Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't have occasion to discuss this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Leaving aside the particular telex, about Mr. Brdjanin in other contexts?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Not directly, but I heard from SDS representatives that Brdjanin was highly respected in the SDS, and that he was deeply appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the positions that the SDS was taking in Kljuc on various matters, did you understand they were making these decisions themselves or from taking instructions from higher levels of authority?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning of work of the joint bodies of the municipal assemblies, most decisions were coordinated with us and the decisions were taken jointly. However, especially at the beginning of 1992, they worked following specific instructions mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how were you able to understand that? How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, and especially when they wanted to change the inscriptions on institutions, the flags and the insignia worn on police uniforms, I had occasion to see this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that, but how did you know that was as a result of instructions from higher levels than the Kljuc municipality itself?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We discussed this at length and we tried to avoid this happening, since the country as such had its own emblems at the level of the country, defined by constitution. However, they wanted to change them and they didn't have any firm arguments in favour, and finally, they said that this was a decision taken by higher levels of authority within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if there is going to be a break, this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break, resuming at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I want to deal now with some of the events from the middle of 1991 until the end, through some of the documents that you personally have knowledge of. Could you be shown, please, Exhibit P853? Now, Mr. Egrlic, this is a document dated the 9th of June, 1991, and it appears to be an official statement number 3 for both the Muslim Bosniak organisation, the MBO, and the SDA, and it talks about effectively it's to do with Martic, Milan Martic. "We are stunned by the impertinence of Martic's military units but even more surprised by the conduct of the legal authorities in Bosansko Grahovo and Titov Drvar and it goes on to say that -- to deplore the behaviour of the Serbs in Titov Drvar and then goes on, "We are prepared to apply the same methods that Martic and his boss, Bajic [phoen], using Knin against the legal authorities of Croatia to welcome those self-proclaimed people's representatives. The guests will be welcomed to the Kljuc commune with barricades and roadblocks because for us, Bosnia and Hercegovina is still the only official homeland and we shall not allow anyone to humiliate it. We call on all patriots to unite in the struggle to preserve the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina regardless of their ethnic, religious, or political affiliation." And I think it's signed -- it's not signed, in fact, but it has your typed signature and that of Mr. Filipovic. Very briefly, Mr. Egrlic, what was this announcement in connection with? What were the events that led to it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: This announcement is a reaction to the events which took place because Martic and others visited Titov Drvar and Bosansko Grahovo and we felt that we should react to that by an announcement and that is what we did. And according -- and this announcement was broadcast over Radio Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And Martic and others were doing what in Titov Drvar and Bosansko Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: They went on a visit to Titov Drvar and Bosansko Grahovo, which was covered quite a lot by the media. They were welcomed there and gratitude was expressed for everything that they were doing in the Republic of Croatia in the Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what made you feel that this threatened the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We felt so because similar attempts were made in relation to joining Kljuc to the Bosanska Krajina region and we felt that this could happen in the region in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, next --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours I'm sorry I missed this on my list but I don't think that it matters much. I think it can go on to the ELMO. It's Exhibit P858. Because I can deal with it briefly. It deals with a topic that the witness has already covered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is another joint announcement in September, 1991 if -- could we just it turn over the page, usher, so that we can see the bottom of it, we can see the date at the bottom? Yeah. 21st of September, 1991. And if we go back to the front page, please? You and the MBO, or your the SDA and the MBO announcing that "The Muslim residents of Kljuc shall stand under no obligation to serve in units of the reserve strength of the Yugoslav army when called up by its organs until a full constitutional order is established in the country. And the Yugoslav army is placed under the command of the socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and not before this war of republics which has been forced upon Croatia ends, we Bosnian Muslims do not wish and shall take no part in this war because we do not consider the war or the Serbian-Croatian conflict our own." And then just if we just turn over again, "We call upon all military conscripts serving on the reserve forces of the police and the Territorial Defence to respond to the mobilisation and report to the above-mentioned forces but only in the area of the Kljuc commune. It is a duty and a honourable obligation for Muslims and people of other ethnic backgrounds to defend our own homes and the homes of our neighbours," et cetera, and it's signed, I think, by you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So do we understand you said that the Muslims didn't respond to mobilisation but you were advising people here to respond to mobilisation but only if it was to serve in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to ask you at this stage, a little bit about the military aspect of things in Kljuc. Did you have, stationed in Kljuc, any units of what was then the 5th Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: In 1991, groups of volunteers were in Kljuc at first, those were the people who went and came back from the front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any regular units of the JNA stationed in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Then parts of the Knin Corps came and stationed themselves at Laniste, about 15 kilometres away from the settlement of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you remember roughly when that was?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: This was probably in March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So up until then, there were no units stationed anywhere near Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: There were no units, but calls were issued for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look, please, then, next at P860?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm confused. He was asked about 5th Corps and then spoke about the Knin Corps. I think those are not the same organisations. I think those are separate organisations, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness, Your Honour but I was going to deal with it because he said that was March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Knin Corps being what, Mr. Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Parts of units who had left Knin and were stationed at the -- in the area of Laniste so these were parts of the units of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know -- and if you do not, say so -- did they come within the 5th Krajina Corps or were they separate?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I'm not able to say that exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour I'm prepared to make that admission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. Is it clear enough for you, Mr. Ackerman? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you look, please, at P860? Is this an announcement -- a public statement made by the SDA on the 24th of September, which in summary says that you, the SDA, invite all political forces active in Kljuc to use your political activity to contribute to keeping this area safe from the storms of war? You invite the Kljuc public security station to direct its activities solely to protecting and keeping safe citizens, persons and properties. Armed groups or paramilitary formations of which there seem to be more and more in our town will be considered undesirable. And three -- item 3, the public security station should recruit necessary staff bearing in mind that the ethnic composition of the police force should correspond to the overall ethnic composition in the commune. Mr. Egrlic what prompted that part of the statement? Item number 3.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The general situation prompted us. The general security situation which was jeopardised in the area of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but in particular, you're asking or you're stating that the police stations should recruit on the basis of the balance of the ethnicities. Was that not happening?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Up until that point, the situation wasn't -- the situation wasn't such that it would indicate that divisions, complete divisions, would occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But was the ethnic composition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this may not be the appropriate time but before Ms. Korner goes on to some other place I need to raise this. I'm wondering with regard to this particular exhibit, Your Honour, if the underlining that we see in the B/C/S version, which has been also put in the translation, if that is on the original. We had this come up before and the Prosecution said they were going to look at the originals that are in some secret vault here to make sure that this wasn't underlining that was done by the Prosecutor's Office but was actually part of the original. I don't know if that's happened with this. I assume it has and I assume the Prosecutor knows the answer to that question but I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman says that but he knows full well that it hasn't been checked and I don't know the answer for sure. I don't think so. I rather feel this was the original but we will check that we will get the original from the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please do. Come back to us on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Egrlic, just this, at this stage in September, 1991, did the police force have a composition that was the equivalent of the ethnic balance in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, not entirely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In which ethnicity was it slanting, was it in favour?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The Serb ethnic group was in a better position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then can we look at item 4? "We resolutely reject the proclamation of the so-called Autonomous Region of Krajina" although it's been translated as district "with its headquarters in Banja Luka as a successor to the Banja Luka community of municipalities and judge the act of its proclamation to be completely unconstitutional and unacceptable to any of the peoples living in the area." And then it goes on to say, "We would like to remind the public that neither the regionalisation issue nor the question of the joining of this commune to the Banja Luka community of municipalities has never been on the agenda of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly, just as the assembly has never adopted any decision which could be interpreted as its consent to the act of joining the autonomous district of Krajina." And then it goes on to say that people in the assembly who declared the autonomy are not the legitimate representatives of Kljuc. Were you aware that people from Kljuc had attended this founding assembly?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: First of all, the decision about joining the municipality of Kljuc to the autonomous region was made amongst the SDS circles and was not discussed by the municipal assembly of Kljuc at this time. 12 Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 10539 to 10543.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. What I'm asking is, did SDS members from the Kljuc assembly attend the founding assembly of the autonomous region, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say that this, as you told us before, threatened the sovereignty and integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in -- goes on finally, at the end of paragraph 4, "In the event that such an illegal decision is implemented by the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Banja Luka, and in the event that they continue with the formation of parastate organs and with putting Muslims in a subordinate position, we shall have to organise a referendum on splitting off to form a separate Muslim commune." Now, at this stage, Mr. Egrlic, had you and the MBO considered setting up a separate Muslim, as it were, municipality in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and we pointed out that in this announcement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why did you feel it was necessary to make this clear?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We wanted to state clearly to the public that we were not in favour of the municipality of Kljuc being joined to the Autonomous Region of Krajina Banja Luka, and that we were committed to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What effect did -- was that going to have in your opinion, if there was this joinder to the autonomous region on the Bosniaks in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The question is not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You were saying you would have to set up a separate Muslim commune, as it was called. Why did you feel that was necessary in the event that the Kljuc municipality was taken into the autonomous region? What effect did you think that would have on Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The effect would be that that municipality, which was within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would have all of its rights, would enjoy all the rights which are guaranteed to it by the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I know he's answered that, Your Honour. He has said that before but what I'm trying to get --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You as a Muslim in a municipality that was taken into this new separatist commune, how was that, did you think, going to affect you personally as a Muslim, if at all?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Since a referendum of the Serbian people was held and that they came out in favour of staying within Yugoslavia, this new parastate did not guarantee that the Muslims would enjoy all of their rights as citizens and for that reason we did not want to accept to remain part of the autonomous region, and that is why we pointed out that the -- we wished to form a separate municipality and that we were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that we wanted to be part of that state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Yes, you can put that document away now. Thank you. Now, you spoke a moment ago about the referendum of the Serbs that took place, which in fact took place after you issued this document, and I don't think there is any dispute it took place in November, 1991. After the referendum had been held, how did that affect the events in the municipality of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: As far as the referendum is concerned, most of the Serbs came out in favour of joining Yugoslavia or in favour of remaining in the former Yugoslavia, and then from that day on, our relationships in the political life of the municipality of Kljuc were disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how were they disrupted in particular?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: They were disrupted in such a way that the municipal assembly didn't work the way it did before, and it was difficult to reach certain decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to look, please, at two further documents connected with the matters that you've dealt with a moment ago. Please, P863. This is a document issued on the 7th of October, 1991, by Banja Luka -- or addressed, I'm sorry it's issued by Kljuc and addressed to the Banja Luka CSB and deals with the ethnicity of the police force, which shows that there was Serbs formed 75 per cent, Muslims 24 per cent and Croats 1 per cent. And goes on to say, "The ethnic composition of members of the police reserve force has been expressed according to the total number of police reservists, despite the fact that the ethnic composition of the police reserve force approximately corresponds to the ethnic composition in the areas in which police stations have been established." And goes on to say that they try and ensure that the composition correspond as closely as possible to the ethnic composition of the population, and it's signed for the chief, Vinko Kondic. By October of 1991, did -- do those figures express what you believe to be the ethnic composition of the police?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I cannot say that with 100 per cent accuracy but most probably they do, because on several occasions, we stated that this balance has been disrupted and that it should be made to reflect the ethnic composition in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. And then could you look at the next document, please, which has actually got two numbers, P90 or 864? We've already been through this, I think, with Mr. Filipovic so I'm just going to ask you to identify it. On the 31st of October, did you issue a joint statement with the MBO, which related to effectively the fax that you've already described to us that you received?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We addressed the public because that was the only way for us to familiarise public opinion with what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, there came a stage in January of 1992 where I think you, the Muslims, did set up what you called the Municipality of Bosnian Kljuc. Would you look just briefly at -- I'm sorry, I just realise I think I made a -- yes. Could you look, please, at P871, first of all? Now, this is a document showing a decision to suspend all activities of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly in the Banja Luka intercommunal regional community, and it's signed by the President of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly, Jovo Banjac. It says it suspends its membership of the intercommunal regional community and says that it will be reinstated as and when the proper decision is taken. Now, do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember how this came about?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the first decision was taken without the municipal assembly meeting, and we reacted to this with a public announcement, under pressure of the public, Mr. Banjac took this decision annulling the initially taken decision, until it could be officially taken at an assembly meeting. A municipal assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, and then on the back of that, if you turn over, we see there was a statement by professor Filipovic which relates to an action that you and the MBO took together.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Asking for a debate in the assembly, in order to avoid our abstaining from participating in the assembly's work. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then -- thank you very much. If we look at what did happen, please, P872. On the 31st of January, I think there was an announcement on Radio Kljuc which effectively stated that there was a newly formed Bosanski Kljuc; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm not going to go through it but it gives at some length the reasons for why you and the MBO decided to take this action. Now, did the assembly that -- as described of Bosanski Kljuc, ever meet?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We just announced that we would form it. We were supposed to hold a referendum of citizens. However, we never managed to do that, in view of the situation, and this municipality of Bosanski Kljuc did not operate, did not function.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can we move, then, into the events before May of 1992? What happened in respect of the police force in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: As regards the police, the request was made by the SDS and the chief of police that the police should change its insignia, those they wore up until then, that is those of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that they should wear new insignia with the national symbol of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the reaction of the SDA and the MBO to that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We tried to have that decision not implemented regarding the change of insignia, on the grounds that we wanted peace and security to be maintained within the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why did you feel that changing the insignia would threaten the peace and security?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We felt it would because policemen who were in the reserve force did not accept wearing such insignia, and one could assume that the police would consist of representatives of one ethnic group only, that is the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you speak to the local leaders of the SDS about that? That is Banjac or Kondic, Veljko?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Of course we did, for several days prior to those changes, we had discussions and sought to avoid this happening. However, ultimately they said it was not up to them, that the order had come from a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did they say who it had come from?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: They said that the order could be changed only by Stojan Zupljanin, the chief of the centre of the security services in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: They offered that we go jointly, that is a delegation, a joint delegation, go to see Stojan Zupljanin and try to dissuade him, not to make those changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you go on that delegation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I was in it and Mr. Omer Filipovic, as well as Jovo Banjac, Vinko Kondic, and Veljko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was Zupljanin's reaction to your visit?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: He received us nicely and he explained that nothing could be done, that it couldn't be changed, and he gave us two berets with the Serbian national symbols as insignia. They said how nice they looked, and after that, we left Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he say why it couldn't be changed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: He didn't elaborate much. This was a very brief meeting, and we found ourselves in an embarrassing situation when he gave us these berets. We realised that there was no way out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And so was this, the insignia, then changed of the police force?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The insignia were changed on the police force and on all public institutions, flags were hoisted with the Serb emblems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, as far as at that stage -- I'm sorry, I should have asked you, roughly, can you remember when that was, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It was exactly on the 7th of May, 1992. I remember that because there was a show of force, because virtually all the features were taken control of and all the main crossroads in town, by the armed forces of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then I want to just go back a couple of months or so to deal with some other events. Firstly, you mentioned that the Knin Corps came to Laniste in March or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there any discussion between yourselves, the SDA, and the SDS, about the arrival of the Knin Corps?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We did have a discussion at a meeting of the national defence council, which in those days was still functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was said at that meeting and by whom?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We were of the opinion that the army should not be positioned there, that there was no need for that, and we asked for an explanation why. We were not given any convincing answers, explaining the need for this, but in view of the members of that body, a vote was taken in favour of positioning the Knin Corps units at Laniste.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the composition of that vote? Who voted in favour? Which party?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: All members of the SDS at the meeting voted in favour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did that make you, the Bosniaks, feel? The arrival of the army at Laniste?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We felt unsafe, as earlier we had seen groups arriving, groups of volunteers, from the front in Croatia, who were not under anybody's control, and we had the feeling that the situation would be further aggravated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once they arrived, in Laniste, were any restrictions placed on the freedom of movement within the Kljuc Municipality?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The more important restrictions were introduced in May, in those days restrictions had not been imposed in the sense of a prohibition of freedom of movement.
